articles.title: Samsung’s Galaxy SmartTag is a $29.99 Tile competitor
articles.summary: The new Galaxy SmartTag tracking device from Samsung lets you locate your lost keys, pets, or whatever else. It uses Bluetooth Low Energy, costs $29.99, and will arrive on January 29th.
articles.body: Alongside the new Galaxy S21 phones and Galaxy Buds Pro, Samsung is announcing a small Bluetooth gadget you can use for locating lost items, just like Tile. It’s called the Galaxy SmartTag, and it will ship beginning on January 29th. It will retail for $29.99, but there’s a decent chance that people who buy a Galaxy S21 phone will end up with some sort of bundled deal that gets it included with purchase. The Galaxy SmartTag works much like a Tile tracker. It’s a small Bluetooth Low Energy (BLE) dongle you attach via a key ring. It pairs with a smartphone via Samsung’s SmartThings app, which can show its last known location on a map. When you’re searching for the tag, the SmartThings app can show a proximity indicator depending on the strength of the BLE signal, and you can tap a button to make the tag emit a chime. One strange decision, though: Samsung tells me the SmartTag will only work with Samsung Galaxy devices. It will not work if you have another Android phone or an iPhone. [Image: Unlike the rumored AirTags from Apple or the rumored next-gen Tile tracker, Samsung’s Galaxy SmartTag doesn’t support Ultra Wideband (UWB). One of UWB’s features is helping objects locate each other in space, so you’d get more data than a proximity meter. It’s a weird miss, too, because Samsung has been including UWB in its phones but hasn’t yet done much to take advantage of that radio (and neither, it should be said, has Apple). Samsung says that a UWB version of the device, called Tag+, will arrive later this year. It will cost $39.99. Both the regular Tag and the Tag+ will be available in multipacks that provide a discount on the cost per tag. [Media: The biggest potential loser in all this is Tile, which has already accused Apple of engaging in anti-competitive behavior. With Samsung also making a directly competitive product, it could put even more pressure on the company. Once upon a time, all Bluetooth headphones worked about the same no matter what phone you used, but lately, both Apple and Samsung have enabled custom features if you buy one of their headphones. It seems possible that the same trend could apply to tracking devices in the not-too-distant future.

articles.title: Anker’s new charger with a screen would feel less gimmicky if it did more
articles.summary: Anker added a screen to the latest version of its tiny 45W Nano charger, but it’s another upgraded feature that makes this a tempting upgrade.
articles.body: The latest Anker 45-watt Nano charger, announced in January, which remains one of the smallest 45-watt chargers on the market, adds a full color screen displaying an animated character and a smattering of details about the device you’re charging. [Product: Anker Nano 45W charger with display | The display is occasionally useful if you like to keep tabs on how much power your device is drawing, but the screen feels more like a marketing gimmick than a feature most consumers will actually benefit from. But it’s not the only upgrade that makes the charger worth considering. The Nano’s hallmark feature is a roughly 1-inch-wide screen that takes up half of the charger’s glossy front panel. These sorts of screens are typically only found on Anker’s larger multi-port power stations, and are frequently limited in what information they display. [Image: Supported devices are identified and briefly named when plugged into the Nano charger. Anker promotes the Nano as “the world’s first smart display charger that knows your iPhone.” When you plug one in, the screen will briefly display your device’s name, then show how much power is being delivered and its battery level. But the charger is limited to Apple hardware and only recognizes a limited number of devices, including iPhone 15 and later models and iPad models from 2020 onward. I tested it with an iPhone 16 Pro and an iPad 10 from 2022, and both were recognized and identified. [Image: The Nano also has a three-stage charging system that adjusts the power delivery rate to help prolong battery life. As the device’s charge level increases, power delivery is reduced. The stages are displayed as “fast,” “steady,” and “trickle” alongside the current wattage and an animated blob-like character whose expression often confuses me. Sometimes it’s sleepy, and other times it appears mad, even if that’s not intentional. When only a USB cable is plugged in, the character will occasionally take a swing at a baseball, or turn into a cookie that opens to reveal fortunes like “fun ahead,” which doesn’t mean anything at all. Tapping a touch-sensitive indent next to the Nano’s USB-C port cycles through two additional screens, including a temperature display and one for switching between charging modes, or you can hold it for two seconds to flip the display 180 degrees as needed. [Image: The Nano charger has three screens showing charging rates, temperature, and charging modes that can be cycled by tapping its touch-sensitive button. [Image: Instead of a touchscreen, the Nano charger has a touch-sensitive button on top (that looks like a dimple) you press to change screens or change modes. The default charging mode is auto (the charger resets to it every time it’s unplugged), and it adjusts the power delivery over time. Care mode reduces the power to help further prolong battery life by keeping your phone cooler. It’s designed for times when you’re not in a hurry to top up your device, such as charging overnight, and it displays the word “gentle” onscreen to remind you to switch to auto mode if you’re in a rush. [Image: Pressing the charger’s touch-sensitive button for two seconds flips the screen 180 degrees so you can reposition its USB-C port. It doesn’t just stop working when connected to devices that aren’t officially supported. I tested it with a Kobo e-reader and a Playdate, and instead of identifying either device, the charger jumped straight to the charging status screen, displaying how much power was being delivered without their battery levels. [Image: The screen-equipped version of the Nano charger (right) is slightly larger and heavier than the version introduced last year (left). The display’s most useful feature is being able to check your iPhone or iPad’s charge level, but that’s information those devices already show. After a few seconds, the Nano charger’s screen automatically turns off, requiring you to reach over to the outlet with a tap to see the charging progress again. You can’t keep the display on at all times, so if your phone or tablet isn’t on the other side of the room and connected via a 60-foot USB cable, why not just reach for your device to check if it’s charged? The Nano’s display would feel less gimmicky if it offered additional functionality, such as an estimate of how long it will take to fully charge, or an option to automatically switch to care mode overnight. [Image: The prongs on the Nano charger can fold flat for travel but also rotate 180 degrees, adding more flexibility for where you can plug it in. The most compelling reason to spend an extra $5 on the new $39.99 Nano charger instead of last year’s $34.99 model is its redesigned folding prongs. They now rotate 180 degrees, so you can plug the charger into an outlet in two different ways to reorient the screen or keep the USB-C port accessible. It’s a simple but clever design change that I wouldn’t be surprised to see Anker incorporate into other smaller chargers in the future. Photography by Andrew Liszewski / The Verge

articles.title: DJI’s Osmo Pocket 4 is a better camera in every respect
articles.summary: The new compact steadicam doesn’t do much the Pocket 3 can’t, but it improves on nearly all of it.
articles.body: First they came for the drones, and now the vlogging cameras. DJI’s Osmo Pocket 4 is the first of its compact steadicams not to launch in the US, following a string of DJI drones also missing the US market. The good news for American buyers is that the Pocket 4 is mostly an evolutionary upgrade, and there’s little it does that the Pocket 3 doesn’t (it looks like the rumored dual-lens Pro version will be more of a reinvention). The good news for everyone else is that those evolutions run throughout the Pocket 4, from the camera sensor to the controls. That makes this an unmistakable improvement over the previous generation. [Product: DJI Osmo Pocket 4 | Stand the Pocket 4 next to 2023’s Pocket 3 and you might not spot the difference. It’s about the same size (only slightly larger and 10g heavier), with a similar rotating screen for both portrait and landscape filming, a control stick and record button beneath that, and an identical gimbal at the top to house the camera. [Image: The two new buttons are welcome, though you’ll still have to navigate a lot of small touchscreen menus. The only real physical difference is a pair of additional buttons underneath the screen, revealed only when it’s flipped horizontally. One is a shortcut for the camera’s zoom controls; the other can be customized to trigger three actions of your choice, locked to a single, double, or triple press. This is oddly and arbitrarily limited, though — only the triple press can be used to change gimbal modes, and that’s the only thing you can set a triple press to do. A little more flexibility would be welcome. It feels fiddly to navigate menus using the 2-inch touchscreen, and better customization could help me do that a whole lot less. [Image: The gimbal hardware is one of the few things that hasn’t changed since the last generation. DJI has also upgraded the camera’s sensor, including its dynamic range, slow-motion capabilities, and low-light performance. Those hardware upgrades are bolstered with new built-in film simulations. Battery life is substantially improved too, and there’s now a generous provision of internal storage in addition to an SD card slot. It’s a more capable, user-friendly camera in almost every respect, even if it looks a lot like what came before. [Video: DJI Osmo Pocket 4] The sensor is the same 1-inch type size as on the Pocket 3, but has otherwise been overhauled. It shoots at a larger resolution, with still photos now at 37 megapixels, way up from 9.4 megapixels before. Video is still capped out at 4K, but the extra pixels means it can now crop into 4x zoom without dropping from 4K, whereas the Pocket 3 was limited to 2x at that resolution. Switching to portrait recording still drops you down to 3K, though. The new sensor has 14 stops of dynamic range, up from 12, and a doubled low-light ISO ceiling of 25,600. Combined, those make for impressive video quality in most lighting. Even in dimly lit London streets close to midnight, the Pocket 4 handled itself well. Direct lights were blown out, and the darker shadows lacked detail, but this would be perfectly usable video for most purposes. [Video: DJI Osmo Pocket 4 low light] The Pocket 4’s stabilization hasn’t been improved as significantly. There are some software tweaks, but it has the same underlying gimbal hardware as the 3. It remains excellent given the camera’s size. It’s easy to get steady handheld video, boosted by effective subject and face tracking, including a Spotlight Follow mode that prioritizes registered faces. It’s great for vlogging, able to keep footage fairly stable when walking about, though this isn’t designed to be an action cam; even a light jog results in pretty shaky video. [Video: DJI Osmo Pocket 4 slow motion] Slow motion has had a big upgrade too. It can now record in 4K resolution at up to 240fps, double what the Pocket 3 offered. It’s only available in landscape mode, though, even at 1080p resolution. Slo-mo does bring with it a small drop in quality and dynamic range, with skies more blown out, but for the most part footage is on par with regular shooting. [Image: [Image: [Image: [Image: Six film simulations, each adjustable in strength, add more versatility to the Pocket 4’s shooting capabilities. Add-ons like the tripod stand and fill light included in DJI’s Creator Combo bundle make it more versatile again, though aren’t necessary for good results. That bundle also includes a DJI Mic 3, and I recommend using it, or another of the company’s wireless microphones, for any video where audio quality matters. The Pocket 4’s built-in microphones aren’t bad at all, and will do a serviceable job in quieter spaces, but they sound tinny when compared to the wireless mic, which does substantially better once you factor in noise cancellation. This is the first Osmo Pocket to offer internal storage, and the 107GB here should be more than enough to avoid ever buying a microSD card. I’ve recorded about 40 minutes of footage while testing the Pocket 4 — mostly 4K, 60fps landscape footage, plus some portrait and slow motion — and used just under 20GB in the process. That was all on a single charge, and I still have about 25 percent left to go. DJI says you can get 240 minutes of use from the camera on a charge, but that’s based on recording 1080p and 24fps footage with both Wi-Fi and the screen off; it seems more realistic to expect an hour or so. [Image: Accessories like the fill light attach using the pins on the gimbal’s rear. While the Osmo Pocket 4 is out now in most of the world, DJI spokesperson Daisy Kong told The Verge that it “will not be available in the US market as the application for authorization is still pending.” So far, there’s not even any sign of it from Xtra, the company that appears to be a DJI shell company and is reselling the Pocket 3 as the Xtra Muse. Xtra is teasing a US launch for a dual-lens steadicam that looks a lot like those leaks of the Osmo Pocket 4 Pro, though, so there’s hope the regular Pocket 4 will make a rebranded appearance too. Outside the US, the Pocket 4 is available in three bundles. The Essential Combo, for £429 / €479 (around $560), includes the Pocket 4 itself, a carrying pouch, and a handle with a 1/4-inch thread for tripod mounting. The £445 / €499 ($585) Standard Combo adds in a wrist strap and a gimbal clamp for safer transportation. Finally, the £549 / €619 ($725) Creator Combo includes a DJI Mic 3 with a magnetic clip and two windscreens, a fill light, a tripod, a wide-angle lens, and a sturdier carrying big to fit it all. The Pocket 4 may be more iterative than innovative, but it’s a top-to-bottom upgrade. There’s scarcely a feature here that hasn’t had some sort of enhancement — even the screen is a few hundred nits brighter than before — so there can be little doubt that this is the best Osmo Pocket yet. If you already own the Pocket 3, or live in the US where that remains the latest option, you’re not missing out on any groundbreaking new features. There’s probably no reason to worry too much about upgrading. But as a package for new buyers, or anyone still on a Pocket 2 or older, DJI has nailed it. Photography by Dominic Preston / The Verge

articles.title: America looks back on 25 years since 9/11
articles.summary: In today’s issue: ▪ A somber anniversary ▪ Conclusion of the RNC midterm convention ▪ Supreme Court rejects Missouri GOP map ▪ Kimmel accuses FCC of threat Americans all around the country today are commemorating the 25th anniversary of the Sept. 11, 2001, terrorist attacks that changed the course of the 21st century. President Trump…
articles.body:
▪ Conclusion of the RNC midterm convention

▪ Supreme Court rejects Missouri GOP map

Americans all around the country today are commemorating the 25th anniversary of the Sept. 11, 2001, terrorist attacks that changed the course of the 21st century.

President Trump will mark the occasion at the Pentagon rather than in New York City, just as he did last year. Vice President Vance will attend New York City’s ceremony at Ground Zero, where the twin towers stood, as will all four living former presidents — Joe Biden , Barack Obama , George W. Bush and Bill Clinton .

In Washington, D.C., all trains and buses will reportedly stop moving for one minute as part of a moment of silence at 9:37 a.m., the minute that the Pentagon was hit by the third hijacked plane.

The attacks, which claimed nearly 3,000 lives as a result of the planes striking the World Trade Center, Pentagon and a field near Shanksville, Pa., dawned a new era that launched the war on terror and transformed the country’s approach to national security and foreign policy.

Thousands more died in the years that followed, suffering from cancer and various respiratory illnesses linked to the toxic air thrown up by the rubble. Controversy surrounding the number of people whose health has been affected — which well exceeds the number that died on Sept. 11, 2001 — resurfaced earlier this week.

New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani (D) released 170,000 pages of records on Tuesday concerning the city government’s response to worsened air quality after the attacks, accusing city leaders of having “lied” about the safety risks.

“People got sick because the leaders they trusted lied and told them they were safe to breathe in toxic air,” Mamdani said at a press conference.

The 9/11 Memorial and Museum estimates more than 400,000 people were exposed to toxic substances from the attacks on the World Trade Center in Manhattan.

Two of those people were Sarah , one of your Morning Report authors,and her twin brother, Jacob . Just shy of four years old, they lived across the street from the twin towers when they collapsed 25 years ago.

In the time since then, their mother was diagnosed with breast cancer and Jacob developed asthma. They believe their conditions are tied to the toxins in the dust from the center.

Sarah recounts her experiences in a personal narrative about her memories of that day, when her family’s home was destroyed and they fled Ground Zero.

“ My memories from that day — some of the earliest I have — are spotty,” she writes. “But an almost-four-year-old’s memories are different from an adult’s — a truth I have come to understand as both a blessing and a curse.”

The Hill’s Bill Sammon , who was present at the Florida elementary school where Bush was reading to schoolchildren when he was told of the attacks, reflects for Insider on how the day transformed Bush from a “sort of caretaker president” into a wartime commander in chief — and his own complicated feelings about the legacy of the wars that followed.

“As the father of a combat Marine who served in both Iraq and Afghanistan, I have mixed feelings about how things turned out,” he writes. “Am I pleased that Saddam’s regime is no more? Absolutely. Am I dismayed that the Taliban is back in power? You bet.”

Much has changed since the worst attack on U.S. soil in history. The Department of Homeland Security (DHS) and Transportation Security Administration (TSA) are now key parts of the government defending the U.S’s national security. They are also routinely closed down in shutdown fights, forcing TSA workers in particular to go to work for weeks at a time without pay, though a move earlier this year to fund DHS through the end of the Trump administration takes that chip off the table for the time being.

Airport security measures were quickly strengthened with metal detectors, bans on bringing liquids over a certain size on planes and a requirement to remove one’s shoes as they passed through lengthy security lines. Those latter two restrictions were added after new attempts were made to take planes down.

As The Hill’s Rebecca Beitsch reports , some of those measures are starting to be pulled back under the second Trump administration. Beitsch notes that while these security measures may have helped prevent another 9/11-like attack, the security constraints have been to the annoyance of millions of travelers. Some of the reforms have been popular, though they have also raised security concerns.

The move from former DHS Secretary Kristi Noem to eliminate shoe removal set off alarms from the Justice Department’s Office of Inspector General, which found full body scanners weren’t always able to see through shoes. Democrats accused Noem of rushing the decision and failing to fully consult with TSA.

Twenty-five years after the attacks that shook America, and fifteen years since Osama bin Laden was killed in a U.S. operation in Pakistan, the fear of it happening again remains a constant force in debates over privacy and security.

As three of our Generation Z editors write in their weekly column “The Feed,” the memories and reactions of older Americans have been engrained in the next generation.

“The events of that day shaped the lives of those born after the terror attacks and grew up watching U.S. troops fight in Iraq, Iran and Afghanistan. Gen Z and Generation Alpha have also lived through the threats from ISIS, al Qaeda and the Taliban,” they write.

Remembrances of 9/11 throughout today will be a stark reminder of all that’s been lost, and what’s stayed with us, since that morning 25 years ago.

▪ The Hill : Poll finds 9/11 among ‘most important historic events’ in adults’ lives.

▪ CBS News : Bush says Americans ‘don’t pay attention to the lesson’ of 9/11.

Trump is vowing to give every adult American $5,000 if Republicans hold the House and Senate in November. The president suggested in a local interview Thursday that he wouldn’t need congressional authority to do so. However, Congress holds the power of the purse. I asked Rep. Adrian Smith (R-Neb.) if he would vote for this promise, and he was noncommittal.

“I want to see details,” Smith said . “The president made a proposal. I’m happy to look at that. The fact is, you know, we legislated on the president’s campaign priorities last time, like no tax on overtime, no tax on tips and no tax on Social Security. Millions of Americans are benefiting from that in a substantive way.”

Republicans will be asked how this squares with traditional conservative principles, including the impact on the national debt. Are they willing to push that aside after making the promise that fiscal responsibility will finally be reined?

Burman hosts “The Hill” weeknights, 6 p.m. EDT/5 p.m. CDT on NewsNation.

The price of a gallon of diesel surpassed $6 for the first time on Friday, according to AAA . The mark is the latest in a series of records for the cost of diesel that have been reached in recent days. The cost of regular gas has also been spiking, reaching almost $4.30 per gallon on average Friday.

The top prosecutor overseeing the Justice Department’s controversial investigations into the president’s adversaries has resigned from the role, he told The Associated Press . Joseph diGenova declined to tell the outlet the circumstances of his departure.

The race for the Senate is so tight , The Hill’s partners at Decision Desk HQ briefly put odds of Democrats taking over the chamber at 51 percent, before shifting things back to the GOP’s favor on Thursday. Just two months ago, DDHQ had placed the GOP’s odds of holding the Senate at 60 percent. Helen Huiskes of The Hill has the full report .

Vice President JD Vance speaks at the Republican convention, Thursday, Sept. 10, 2026, in Dallas. (AP Photo/Julia Demaree Nikhinson)

‘ALL ABOUT VANCE’ : The second and final day of the GOP’s midterm convention wrapped up Thursday with a rousing speech from the vice president as talk is on the rise about his possible 2028 prospects.

Vance delivered the keynote address, a speech that at one point was interrupted with chants of “48.” He brushed off the calls, saying the Republicans must first “take care of business” in November before worrying “about what comes next.”

Attendees told The Hill’s Julia Mueller , who was reporting from the convention in Dallas, that they have their eye on Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio for 2028.

“All about Vance,” said Texan Martha McCullough .

“Either one of ’em,” said Dedra Taie , also from Texas.

Vance sought to draw a contrast between Republicans and Democrats in his address, branding Democrats as extremists, as many speakers did during the convention.

“I’m not asking you to agree with every policy of our administration. I’m asking you to recognize the contrast with the radicals, and the achievements of the last 18 months,” he said.

Several other potential White House contenders, including Sen. Ted Cruz (R-Texas) and Donald Trump Jr. , also spoke on the second day.

The president returned to the stage for closing remarks , calling on attendees to make a pledge to vote in November.

“Please raise your right hand,” he said.

“I pledge to the greatest president in the history of the United States that loves us so much he can’t even breathe, that I will go out with my family, my friends.”

▪ The Hill : Vance takes aim at James Talarico in speech.

The New York Times : Vance relishes the spotlight at Trump’s convention

BIPARTISAN BACKLASH : The president’s promise to send $5,000 to every U.S. adult if Republicans maintain control of both chambers of Congress in November is facing pushback from across the aisle .

Fiscal conservatives questioned how the federal government could afford to pay the 270 million Americans so much money. Rep. Chip Roy (R-Texas) estimated that the plan would cost about $1.2 trillion.

“Maybe some of us think dependency is evil & soul-sucking in all its forms,” he said in a post on social media.

Marc Short , who served as Trump’s legislative affairs director during his first term, said Trump’s pledge further removes his administration from “fiscal responsibility.”

Meanwhile, other critics like Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.) argued the plan amounted to bribery. Former Rep. Bob Good (R-Va.), who chaired the House Freedom Caucus, called Trump’s plan a “socialist vote-buying scheme.”

Trump defended the plan’s timing in an interview with Fox News that aired Thursday night, arguing that the country can afford it because of the money being taken in from tariffs.

The proposal still has some support, as Sen. Bernie Moreno (R-Ohio) said he would prepare legislation so the “Trump dividend” is passed “immediately” after the midterms.

▪ Reuters : Is the dividend legal and how would it work?

CLAMPING DOWN : The Supreme Court blocked an order Thursday that had directed Missouri to go forward with a new congressional map that would have likely netted Republicans an extra House seat in November.

The court didn’t publicly explain its decision, and no justice noted a dissent. With the ruling lifting a federal judge’s order, that leaves a state court’s directive in place that officials use the current congressional map, which has a breakdown of six Republican and two Democratic representatives.

The federal judge’s order had sparked confusion about what boundaries would be used in November.

The high court’s ruling marked the second time in less than a week that it weighed in to turn away efforts for Republicans to implement the 7-1 map. It was handed down just moments before the Missouri Supreme Court held a hearing on whether Missouri Secretary of State Denny Hoskins (R) should be held in contempt for directing local officials to proceed with the new map.

The conclusion of the week brings an end to a chaotic series of days in the Show Me State as the clock is ticking before the first mail-in ballots are set to be sent out Sept. 19. At least for now, the 6-2 map is what’s set to be used, which is good news for Rep. Emanuel Cleaver (D-Mo.), whose district is most affected by the changes.

▪ St. Louis Public Radio : Hoskins agrees to use old map.

▪ The Hill : Appeals court denies Trump’s mail-in ballot restrictions.

FCC VS. KIMMEL : Late-night host Jimmy Kimmel said an interview he conducted with Texas Democratic Senate nominee James Talarico will not air on broadcast because of a threat from the Federal Communications Commission (FCC).

Kimmel told his audience Wednesday that he has interviewed candidates for office for decades without issue. He said that included Trump on multiple occasions.

“But now that he’s president, something has changed,” Kimmel said. “His FCC has threatened me, threatened my show, threatened our network … based on simple editorial decisions.”

Kimmel said the conversation will instead be published in its entirety on the show’s YouTube channel.

Kimmel has clashed with the FCC before, as Chair Brendan Carr called for Kimmel to be fired last year over comments he made following the assassination of conservative activist Charlie Kirk .

An interview that former late-night host Stephen Colbert conducted with Talarico earlier this year also was pulled from the air and instead posted on YouTube. CBS denied an accusation from Colbert that the network prevented the interview from airing.

The president and first lady Melania Trump will participate in a 9/11 observance ceremony at the Pentagon at 9 a.m. and a wreath-laying ceremony at 10:25 a.m. He will participate in signing time at 2:30 p.m. and later depart the White House to travel to Dublin, Ireland, for the weekend, where will meet with Irish officials and attend the final round of the Irish Open.

A video featuring Sen. John Fetterman (D-Pa.) plays at the Republican convention on Sept. 9, 2026, in Dallas. (Alex Brandon, Associated Press)

WHAT COMES NEXT : Sen. John Fetterman ‘s (D-Pa.) surprise appearance on the first day of the GOP’s midterm convention is adding to questions about what comes next for the senator increasingly on the outs with his own party.

The Hill’s Alexander Bolton reports Democrats in Washington are growing more exasperated with Fetterman over his frequent Fox News appearances and critiques of democratic socialists.

Strategists and analysts said Fetterman’s low approval rating among Pennsylvania Democrats already has made him winning reelection in 2028 difficult. And now, one Democratic strategist said Fetterman’s virtual convention appearance is “pouring gasoline on the fire.”

Fetterman sent in a video to introduce his fellow Pennsylvania senator, Dave McCormick (R), with whom he’s grown closer in recent months. In the message, Fetterman described himself as a “common sense” Democrat and continued his criticisms of the Democratic Party’s left wing.

Following the day’s events, Fetterman confirmed he would continue to caucus with the Democrats in the Senate and would support Democrats if they win back control of the Senate in November.

But the decision to make a high-profile cameo at the convention is being viewed as a major provocation by some Democrats, Bolton reports.

DENVER SUES DHS: The city of Denver has filed a lawsuit against DHS and Secretary Markwayne Mullin to try to block Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officers from showing up at voting sites during elections.

The lawsuit, filed Thursday, claims that ordering federal officers to detain individuals and serve warrants at polling sites violates the “troops at polls” law, which was enacted during the Civil War and prohibits federal officers from showing up to “any place where a general or special election is held, unless such force be necessary to repel armed enemies of the United States.”

Mullin contends that his policy would only allow officers to show up at polling sites “if there is a threat to that polling place or we’re serving a warrant on someone that we have been actively tracking down.”

The city, however, dismissed the claim, citing DHS’s “failure to engage in reasoned decision making and disregard for existing federal law.” Denver pointed to violent encounters involving ICE officers — including two notable instances in which U.S. citizens were killed — and reporting that documented more than 170 examples of ICE officers detaining U.S. citizens.

The lawsuit comes as Democrats have sounded the alarm about the potential for law enforcement officers to intimidate voters during the midterms.

Denver Mayor Mike Johnston (D) said Thursday that stationing officers near polling places “is only meant to scare people and suppress votes,” adding, “We’ll fight tooth and nail to prevent it.”

Sharing the memory in a social media post addressed to Rohit Shetty, Orry recalled how, a couple of years ago, a small mention of him appeared in a newspaper article. Excited by the mention, he called Janhvi to ask whether he should share it on social media. He recalled that Janhvi laughed and told him, “Lol Orry, no... one day you will be front page on your own merit and I would want you to post that.”Sharing a series of newspaper cutouts featuring his mentions, Orry wrote, “Dear Rohit Ji, A couple years ago there was a tiny skinny little sliver of a mentions of me in random newspaper in an article, thrilled I called up my close personal friend @janhvikapoor and asked if I should post it. She chuckled and said “lol Orry no..one day you will be front page on your own merit and I would want you to post that”.. I cannot lie, I did get a little sad because I truly doubted if that day would ever come..”“Cut to last year where i seemed to live on the front and back page of every paper for a series of unfortunate infamous baseless articles that they might as well have listed my public service industry career in the obituaries. My only accomplishment was that I had become the face of fake news.”He added, “This year I am finally f*ing front page for nothing notorious, my KKK journey being a matter of pride and my accomplishments being discussed throughout the nation.. showcasing me as more than just a privileged self-made nepo baby. I am ever so grateful for this platform and so grateful to @janhvikapoor for believing & seeing potential in me back then and now.”Interestingly, Orhan and Janhvi share a close, family-like friendship that dates back nearly a decade. articles.title: Maria Bartiromo breaks silence after abrupt Fox News departure
articles.summary: Maria Bartiromo thanked supporters and teased her "next moves" in her first public statement since her abrupt Fox News departure.
articles.body:
Maria Bartiromo is signaling that she has more in store after her abrupt departure from Fox News .

The veteran television anchor addressed the situation publicly for the first time on Thursday, Sept. 10, one week after Fox News Media announced it had parted ways with her after more than 12 years.

"Before too much time passes, I want to thank all of my friends, followers and supporters for all of the kind words," Bartiromo wrote in an Instagram post ⁠. "I am so grateful for the outpouring of love this past week on social media & through texts. I love you all and I promise to be back soon w my next moves."

The post included a series of peaceful snapshots featuring flowers, a beach sunset and Bartiromo's dog, Dusty. She concluded the message by writing, "Sending love from @Dustybsteinberg & me."

Bartiromo, 58, shared a similar message on X alongside a photo of a rainbow breaking through the clouds. After thanking her supporters again, she teased: "More to come."

The posts did not reveal what Bartiromo plans to do next or directly address the circumstances surrounding her Fox departure.

Fox News Media announced Sept. 3 that Bartiromo was no longer with the company, effective immediately. The network did not provide a reason for the decision, describing it as a business matter and thanking her for her work.

However, Bartiromo's attorney, Bryan Freedman, has challenged reports characterizing her departure as a firing. In a statement provided to USA TODAY , Freedman said "the irresponsible reports that have been published stating that Maria Bartiromo was fired or is no longer an employee of Fox are absolutely and unequivocally false."

"Make no mistake, we have the receipts and witnesses and they will come out whether through the courthouse or otherwise," Freedman continued.

Bartiromo joined Fox in 2014 after two decades at CNBC. She hosted three programs across Fox News and Fox Business: "Mornings with Maria," "Maria Bartiromo's Wall Street" and "Sunday Morning Futures."

Following the announcement, Fox removed Bartiromo's name from its business programs and began using replacement hosts. Her departure also prompted a public reaction from President Donald Trump , who praised her professionalism and described her as a "true warrior."

Although Bartiromo has not offered details about her split with Fox, her latest messages suggest she does not intend to remain away from the public eye for long.

Contributors: Kalia Richardson, USA TODAY.

articles.title: Why Apple’s next computer should be for the smart home
articles.summary: After the “intelligent personal hub,” Apple needs to build the intelligent home hub.
articles.body: John Ternus didn’t mention Apple Home once during his first keynote as Apple CEO. But he did open by describing an “intelligent personal hub” that prioritizes local processing, protects your privacy, and integrates with all your other devices, apps, and services. While Ternus was talking about the iPhone — not a new smart home device — what he spelled out is exactly what I want to see Apple make: an intelligent home hub, a computer for your home. Rumors suggest Apple’s first smart home hub with a screen is imminent. While that’s long overdue, it’s likely to be more interface than infrastructure, a device that can run your home locally but still uses the cloud. What the smart home needs is a computer to run it — one that controls and processes data from connected devices locally, improving speed, reliability, and privacy while securely storing your digital life, from photos and files to music and movies. Crucially, it would do all this inside your home. The cloud has worked well for years, but the recent proliferation of AI-powered home features, such as generating text descriptions from security camera footage, makes local computing more compelling. On-device processing can be faster and more private, and it depends less on an internet connection. These features will also evolve quickly to feed more context to our smart homes, bringing more utility but also a greater need for privacy and security. [Image: The category of smart home super hubs emerged at IFA in Berlin this month. This is the Anker Eufy MindBase, a smart home hub that supports dual-band Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, Thread, and Zigbee, and is a Matter controller. It runs an on-device, Anker-developed LLM with support for 16 wireless cameras with expandable local storage up to 48 TB. This type of dedicated home computer — or smart home brain — was an emerging category at last week’s IFA consumer tech show. Anker launched its Eufy MindBase home hub, and Ugreen debuted its HomeAgent, both combining network-attached storage, local AI to process and store footage from cameras, with a smart home hub to connect all your devices. But one piece is still missing: networking. Most home routers haven’t caught up with today’s smart home. Despite years of talk about smarter routers, manufacturers and ISPs still seem reluctant to take on the complexity. Comcast has had Thread and Matter support in its gateways since 2022, but hasn’t turned them on. Connecting devices to your home network remains one of the most frustrating parts of the smart home, with manufacturers, ISPs, and platforms all pointing fingers when things fail. Ikea’s recent troubles rolling out new Matter-over-Thread devices are just one example. Here’s where Apple could step in and combine all three — a smart home hub, local storage with AI processing capabilities, and a home router — into one device. A hub. AI. A router. Are you getting it? Call it an Apple Home Server. There’s no evidence Apple is building such a thing. But the company’s recent contributions to OpenWrt, the open-source software that powers most routers, could be a tentative first step. One Apple box for your home: Connect it to your modem, and it becomes your Wi-Fi router, Matter Controller, Thread border router, smart home hub, private AI computer, and home server. It stores your files, photos, music, and movies; processes your camera footage locally; runs your automations even when the internet is down; and optionally backs everything up to iCloud. It wouldn’t be another smart home hub; it would be the computer your home needs. Plug it in, sign in with your Apple account, and it just works. That last part is crucial, and plays directly to Apple’s strength: hardware that is “super easy to use without a big learning curve,” as Ternus put it this week. Apple also has experience combining these pieces. AirPort Express put networking and media streaming on one box; AirPort Extreme and Time Capsule added NAS capabilities; and HomeKit Secure Routers brought Apple’s security into the network itself. Apple walked away from all these products in 2018, saying at the time it might return to the space if it found a meaningful way to progress routers further. The pieces have never fit together more perfectly than they do now. [Image: Apple’s Airport Express is a much-missed device. Resurrecting it as part of a powerful whole-home computer for today’s smart home setups would be a popular move. Apple is deeply involved in developing Matter and is spearheading the Thread networking protocol. An Apple Home Server could bring the entire smart home stack together, letting Apple control everything end to end and remove much of the complexity. Matter even has a blueprint for part of this device: the Matter Home Router Access Point device type combines Wi-Fi networking and Thread Border Router functionality, and Apple’s contributions to OpenWrt focus on HRAP implementation. According to reporting by Matter Alpha, Apple’s code includes production-grade networking infrastructure that could be turned into a consumer product. There’s no evidence that’s what Apple is doing; it could simply be for router manufacturers. But the pieces are falling into place. With Apple bringing Apple Intelligence to its HomeKit Secure Video service in iOS 27, a Home Server device could take that service to the next level with fully local processing. Local is the key. An Apple Home Server would be a supercharged Apple Home Hub, powering local-first smart home automations, keeping data private and secure at home, and improving responsiveness for devices like smart lights, locks, and security cameras. It could work alongside existing home hubs — the HomePod, Apple TV, and rumored HomePad — for voice and screen interfaces. This might go against the grain. Apple loves subscriptions. But it loves its premium hardware even more, and this would undoubtedly be premium hardware. Also, a device like this would give Apple a powerful foundation for everything it does in the home: iPhones, Macs, iPads, Apple TVs, HomePods, its existing digital services, and potential future AI-powered ones. And, unlike a typical smart home hub, it could appeal to anyone who wants a reliable, private home router and a way to store their digital life at home. Smart home infrastructure is broken, and Apple is uniquely positioned to fix it. An Apple Home Server is the hardware backbone Apple Home has always needed. As our digital lives move deeper into the cloud and AI makes the smart home more dependent on data, the case for a computer to run our homes gets stronger, and building one on open standards could limit lock-in. Apple has all the pieces. The smart home has been waiting for someone to put them together. If Apple finally builds it, the only surprise will be that it took this long.

articles.title: 8 biggest things we learned from Apple's 2026 event
articles.summary: iPhone Duo opens to a 7.6-inch foldable display starting at $1,999, but Siri Recap's ambient listening on Apple Watch may spark privacy concerns.
articles.body: Apple finally did it. After years of watching Samsung, Google and other phone makers experiment with foldables, Apple has entered the race with iPhone Duo, its first foldable iPhone. It's the announcement everyone is talking about, but it was hardly the only thing that stood out. Apple also showed us an iPhone camera that can help prove a photo is authentic. Siri AI is getting far more personal. Apple Watch will soon be able to summarize conversations you want to remember. Even AirPods are getting smarter at a lower starting price. Some of these upgrades feel genuinely useful. Others raise questions about privacy, price and how much intelligence we want built into the devices around us. So, after sorting through everything Apple announced, here are the eight biggest things we learned from Apple's 2026 event and what they could mean for you. Missed CyberGuy LIVE? Watch the Protect Your Money replay Our free CyberGuy LIVE class, Protect Your Money From Today’s Biggest Threats, has ended, but you can still watch the full replay and download our financial protection checklist. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you through five simple ways to help defend yourself against AI scams, fraud, identity theft and financial hacks. You’ll learn how to set up bank alerts, strengthen your account logins, protect your phone number, freeze your credit and help secure your retirement savings against unauthorized transfers. No technical experience is needed. Get the free replay and checklist now at CyberGuyLive.com IS APPLE INTELLIGENCE ON YOUR IPHONE REALLY SECURE? 1) iPhone Duo is Apple's big foldable swing Let's start with the product everyone is talking about. iPhone Duo opens to a 7.6-inch Super Retina XDR display. Apple says that gives you 50% more screen area than iPhone 18 Pro Max. The 5.4-inch outer display offers 90% of the screen area of iPhone 18 Pro. Apple also tackled one of the biggest complaints about foldables: the crease. The company developed a custom nano-texture finish that reduces glare and reflections. Apple says the finish also minimizes the visibility of the crease while giving the display a matte feel. There are some other unexpected choices. Instead of Face ID, iPhone Duo uses Touch ID built into the side button. You can enroll multiple fingers, so unlocking works in different positions. Apple Pencil with USB-C support will arrive later this year. The phone uses Grade 5 titanium. Apple also says it carries an IP68 rating for dust and water resistance. The folding design also creates some camera tricks you can't get on a regular iPhone. Dual Capture can show your front and rear camera feeds at the same time during FaceTime, while Duo FaceTime lets someone beside you join the call using the outer display. You can also use that outer screen to frame higher-quality selfies with the rear cameras. Apple added a few other clever touches. Duo Preview lets the person you're photographing see the shot before you take it, while Kid Cue uses animations to get a child's attention. Smart Take can even watch the scene and automatically snap a photo when everyone is ready. Then comes the part that may give you sticker shock: the price. iPhone Duo starts at $1,999 with 256GB of storage. Apple will offer configurations up to 2TB. Preorders begin Oct. 16, with availability starting Oct. 23. 2) Apple redesigned iOS around the fold The hardware grabs your eye, but the software could decide whether Duo succeeds. Apple changed iOS 27 so content moves between the outside and inside displays. Open the phone and apps can expand onto the larger screen. You can also put two apps side by side. Mail can show your inbox alongside a message. The Home Screen can display two pages at once. The system also responds when you fold or rotate the phone. That caught my attention because a folding screen needs to earn its extra cost. If I open a phone this large, I want more than a bigger version of the same app. Apple is also giving developers tools to take advantage of the design. During the event, Apple showed Zoom using the expanded screen for video calls and Netflix adapting its experience to the two displays. The cameras use the second screen too. Duo Preview lets the person you're photographing see themselves on the outer display. Meanwhile, Smart Take can follow a scene and automatically snap the photo when everyone looks ready. Those are the features that could make the folding design useful after the initial wow factor wears off. 3) iPhone 18 Pro gets much more serious about photography If a foldable phone doesn't interest you, Apple gave the regular Pro lineup a substantial camera upgrade. The iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max use a 48MP Fusion Main camera with a variable aperture. The camera can automatically adjust the aperture depending on lighting and depth of field. Apple also gives photographers manual control through four aperture settings: ƒ/1.48, ƒ/1.8, ƒ/2.8 and ƒ/4.0. In darker environments, opening the aperture lets in more light. A narrower aperture can keep more of a scene in focus. However, another camera feature may prove even more important. Apple Reference Image securely signs photo data at the pixel level when the picture is captured. Apple says that can help verify exactly what the camera sensor saw. Think about where we're headed with AI-generated images. Being able to verify that an image began as an actual camera capture could become valuable for journalists, investigators or anyone documenting something important. That feature may get less attention than the new camera hardware. I wouldn't overlook it. iPhone 18 Pro starts at $1,199, while iPhone 18 Pro Max starts at $1,299. Preorders begin Sept. 12, with both phones available starting Sept. 18. APPLE RAISES PRICES AS AI CHIP COSTS SURGE 4) Battery life may be the iPhone 18 Pro upgrade you feel most Apple can show us faster chips every year. Most of us notice battery life much faster. Apple says the iPhone 18 Pro Max can deliver up to 45 hours of video playback, the longest battery life the company has offered in an iPhone. It also rates the Pro Max for up to 30 hours of general use per charge. Charging gets faster too. Apple says iPhone 18 Pro can reach 50% charge in around 15 minutes with a compatible adapter. Underneath it all sits the A20 Pro chip. Apple built A20 Pro using 2-nanometer technology. The chip includes a second Neural Engine, bringing the total to 32 Neural Engine cores. Apple says that doubles compute power for advanced on-device models. The new Pro models also use a redesigned vapor chamber to manage heat. Faster performance sounds good. More time away from a charger is something you'll notice every day. 5) Siri AI is moving from keynote promise to everyday use Siri AI had a big role in Apple's Sept. 9 iPhone 18 Pro unveiling. Apple showed how its rebuilt assistant can use your personal context, understand what you're looking at and take action across the apps you already use. During the event, Apple showed someone asking what her mother wanted to cook during an upcoming visit. Siri searched Mail and Messages to find the answer. Apple also demonstrated Siri working through the Camera app. Point your iPhone at something and Siri can answer questions about what you're seeing or take action based on what's around you. There's also a new Siri app on the Home Screen. You can use it to start a conversation or return to an earlier one, with conversations syncing privately through iCloud. Siri AI begins rolling out in beta in English on Sept. 14 with iOS 27. Apple says support for French, Japanese, Korean, Portuguese and Spanish will follow in October. 6) Siri Recap may start a big privacy conversation This one made me pay attention. Apple announced Siri Recap for Apple Watch Series 12 and Apple Watch Ultra 4. It uses ambient listening to turn conversations into high-level notes. Apple says each recap can include a title, summary and key points that appear in the Siri app. You control where and when Siri Recap takes notes. For example, you could allow it at work but disable it at night. Then there is Live Rewind. Double-click the Digital Crown and Apple Watch can transcribe what was said during the previous 15 seconds. You can then review what you missed. That's useful if you missed something someone said in a noisy restaurant. Naturally, ambient listening raises privacy questions. Apple says these Audio Intelligence features do not create or store audio recordings. The company says raw audio used for processing remains inaccessible, even to Apple. Apple also says Audio Intelligence does not identify or attribute speakers. Live Rewind transcripts and Siri Recaps use end-to-end encryption when syncing through iCloud. Siri Recap and Live Rewind require Siri AI. Apple says both will arrive in beta later this year, starting in English. I like the idea of getting help remembering an important conversation. However, I would want to know exactly when the feature is active every time I use it. 7) Apple Watch gets smarter about your health Apple Watch is becoming more aggressive about turning health data into something you can understand. Series 12 and Ultra 4 use Apple's new Health Sensing System. According to Apple, Apple Watch Series 12 can now measure heart rate every five seconds throughout the day. Apple also says heart rate variability is measured up to 24 times more often than before. Apple says its head-to-head testing found the system delivered the most accurate heart rate sensing in a wearable. For everyday users, Readiness may be the more relatable feature. Each morning, Apple Watch analyzes your recent activity, sleep and vital signs. It then gives you a score designed to help you decide whether to push harder or recover. The score can also change during the day. Meanwhile, Apple Watch Ultra 4 gets up to 50 hours of normal use. Max Extended Workout mode can reach 45 hours. Apple Watch Series 12 starts at $399, while Apple Watch Ultra 4 starts at $799. Both are available to preorder now and will be available starting Sept. 18. Apple also showed how the iPhone and Apple Watch can work together to assess how your body is moving. With Movement Evaluations in the redesigned Health app, you can position your iPhone so the camera can see you, then follow guided exercises while vision-based AI analyzes your movements. Apple says the assessments can look at flexibility, strength, balance, movement mechanics and VO2 max. They can also help you track your progress while recovering from an injury. Apple says the processing happens on your device, and no video is recorded, stored or shared. SAMSUNG GALAXY Z FOLD8 LINEUP ADDS THREE CHOICES 8) AirPods 5 could be one of the event's better values The final surprise may appeal to people who have no interest in spending $1,999 on a foldable phone. Apple announced AirPods 5 with Active Noise Cancellation for $129. Apple says the new earbuds provide stronger Active Noise Cancellation than the previous generation. They keep an open-ear design for people who prefer not to use silicone ear tips. The standard $129 model gets up to four hours of listening with ANC enabled. The charging case brings the total to up to 20 hours. A $149 version adds volume swipe on the stem and a wireless charging case. It gets up to five hours per charge with ANC and up to 22 hours with the case and ANC enabled. Both versions are available starting Sept. 18, with preorders open now. AirPods 5 also support Live Translation and Siri AI. During the event, Apple showed AirPods translating Spanish into English while the wearer continued a face-to-face conversation. Compared with iPhone Duo, AirPods 5 may seem like a smaller announcement. Still, the $129 model could end up being one of the products far more people actually buy. Kurt's key takeaways Apple gave us plenty to talk about, but iPhone Duo is the one people are going to want to pick up and play with. I certainly do. At $1,999, it carries a premium price, but Apple is clearly betting that the larger screen and new foldable experiences will be enough to tempt early adopters. What interests me more is how much smarter these devices are becoming. Siri AI finally looks like it could understand enough about your day to be genuinely helpful. Siri Recap sounds incredibly convenient too, but a watch that can summarize conversations around you deserves some healthy scrutiny about when it's listening and how clearly you know it's active. Then there are improvements you don't need a demo to appreciate. Give me longer iPhone battery life any day. And Apple Reference Image could become far more important than it sounds today if we reach a point where you can no longer trust your eyes to tell whether a photo is real. After everything Apple announced, what would actually convince you to upgrade, and what would make you hold onto the device you already have? Let us know by writing to us at CyberGuy.com. articles.title: Meta may have leaked the first look at its slim ‘Project Phoenix’ headset
articles.summary: Ahead of Meta Connect images leaked online seemingly revealing the design for the company’s “Project Phoenix” headset with a slimmer frame than its Quest 3.
articles.body: Just a couple of weeks before Meta Connect starts on September 23rd, UploadVR posted images seemingly revealing the design for Meta’s “Project Phoenix” headset. The images, which UploadVR says were “found in the HorizonOS Prescription Lens firmware package,” suggest Meta may be looking to compete with devices like those from Xreal or Viture. These companies’ mixed reality glasses are a bit bulkier than something like Meta’s Ray-Ban AI smart glasses, but a step down from a full VR headset like Meta’s Quest 3. This leak shows something that’s almost in between larger headsets and smart glasses, with lenses set into a slim, glasses-style frame. A shot from behind shows a wire extending from one of the earpieces, possibly for a battery or compute puck. There also appear to be outward- and downward-facing cameras in the earpieces. Project Phoenix has been in the works for a while now, and isn’t expected to launch until next year. Google is also working on a pair of Project Aura XR glasses in a similar vein, with an external compute puck that’s wired to the frames.

articles.title: Microsoft’s head of comms is leaving after almost 20 years
articles.summary: Frank Shaw has been supporting Microsoft’s communications for nearly 30 years.
articles.body: Frank Shaw is leaving Microsoft after 17 years as chief communications officer. In an internal note to his team, Shaw says he’s “decided it is time for me to move on and try new things,” after supporting Microsoft’s communications for 29 years — nearly 20 years as a Microsoft employee plus time at the Waggener Edstrom agency (now We. Communications) before that. Shaw has been at the heart of Microsoft’s communications since 1997, helping the company navigate multiple Windows and Office releases, CEO transitions, the all-important bet on cloud, and huge acquisitions like the $26.2 billion LinkedIn purchase in 2016 and the $69 billion acquisition of Activision Blizzard in 2023. He’s well-respected across the public relations industry, and PRWeek recently named him number one on its 2026 list of the most powerful people in the PR industry. Internally at Microsoft he’s also well-respected among executives, and has built up a reputation for being direct, but respectful. Many employees have told me over the years that they always fear an email from him for misspeaking or accidentally leaking product plans. He’s earned a reputation outside of the company as someone who is always willing to argue with critics, correct stories, and defend Microsoft. In 2013, he ripped into Apple and the press for daring to compare iWork to Office, and he regularly appears on X to shoot down rumors or to correct information about Microsoft. At Microsoft’s 50th birthday party last year, he appeared onstage to read out a series of hilarious mean tweets about his PR activities. I’ve been covering Microsoft for more than 25 years, and I first encountered Shaw as a naive teenager trying to get into blogging. I would post confidential Microsoft documents online at my time at Neowin, or blog about early Windows features before the company was ready to announce them. That regularly got me into trouble with Microsoft’s army of lawyers, and even got Neowin knocked offline for 24 hours. Despite there being a great deal of mutual respect between us, I’ve upset Shaw plenty of times over the decades, leading to some heated debates or disagreements over stories. Still to this day, when Frank calls my phone, I brace myself, knowing Microsoft is either about to announce something crazy or I’ve upset the company again. But what’s he doing next? Shaw isn’t retiring just yet, but he tells me he’s going to take a well-earned break before moving on to “other things” he wants to do. Could that be PR for an AI startup? Baking sourdough bread professionally? In a manner befitting a communications professional: He refuses to tell me. Microsoft isn’t naming a replacement for Shaw yet, as he’s not leaving the company until the end of the year. “I’ll be here through the end of the calendar year, and the company is working through next steps, look for an update in the next few weeks,” says Shaw in a note to his team. Here’s Shaw’s full internal memo to his communications team: > (don’t bury the lede) > After 17 years in this role and nearly 29 working with the company, I’ve decided it is time for me to move on and try new things. Takeshi and I have been talking about this for a while, and I am excited about what’s next, for me and for Microsoft. I remain optimistic about the company mission, the incredible talent on this team, and how much the company depends on us during this critical time. I’ll be here through the end of the calendar year, and the company is working through next steps, look for an update in the next few weeks. I know you will have many questions, and I’m looking forward to talking to you at our AMA here later this morning <link> > (start burying) > A while back, there was a social media trend where people answered the question, “What topic could you give a 30-minute presentation on with no preparation?” Me, I could talk about the US Marines, the changing nature of influence, sourdough starter, the Oregon Ducks, but my go to would have to be aspects of Stephen King’s the Dark Tower books, starting with “The Gunslinger;” the question then becomes which particular aspect. A quick primer, the series follows Roland Deschain, the last of the gunslingers (a mix between mayor/judge/sheriff), as he chases the man in black through time and dimensions in a quest to save the world. The question embedded throughout is if it is possible for Roland to retain his identity and meaning in a world that had moved on. The refrain is that the world moves on, move with it or fall. Can Roland move and grow, or will he be stuck? One of the concepts that sticks with me comes as we are introduced to more characters, now moving with Roland. He introduces the concept of ‘ka-tet’ to describe them. ‘Ka’ is essentially fate, or destiny, and ‘tet’ translates to a group of people, put together for a larger meaning – a group brought together with a shared mission and destiny, a group with shared goals, the willingness to sacrifice for those goals, with a deep emotional connection to each other and the ability to make and act on decisions with what can feel like supernatural speed. > I’ve always loved the evolution from the solo gun slinger we meet in book one to the team that operates throughout the later books. Roland on his own was formidable but failed in his missions, as part of a ka-tet he was in the end successful. > You, my friends, are my ka-tet. Together, we’ve accomplished amazing things. My gratefulness is endless. > We will have time together still over the next set of months as we finalize decisions and deliver great work on behalf of the company, and I will be close by after. In the Dark Tower, the traditional departure saying is “long days and pleasant nights,” and so it will be, but not until December. 😊 > fxs

articles.title: We unfolded the iPhone Duo
articles.summary: On The Vergecast: a deep dive into the iPhone Duo, Apple Watches, and LLMs on the Mac
articles.body: You only get one chance at a first impression, and getting to introduce Apple’s first folding phone is certainly a strong way to start things off as Apple’s CEO. On The Vergecast today, we’re talking all about Apple’s launch event: how John Ternus did in his first appearance as CEO, what we make of the new iPhones, and whether Apple is stepping into dangerous territory with its new AI features on the Apple Watch. First up, Allison Johnson joins me to discuss the new iPhones, which she had a chance to test in Cupertino. Both of us have some questions about the new variable aperture camera on the iPhone 18 Pro — and whether the real upgrade simply lies in the wider aperture, not the ability to stop it down. Then we dig into the iPhone Duo and how Apple decided to pick and choose the best parts of Android foldables. Watch | Listen | Get ad-free After that, Victoria Song joins me to discuss the new Apple Watches, which she also had a chance to test out. We dive into the new sensor array and whether it allows for legitimately new metrics or just more vibesy health data. And then we both break down a little while figuring out what it means that Apple added the ability for both new Apple Watches to have an always-on microphone that summarizes all of your conversations. This is an Apple-packed episode, so from there we jump to a special segment with Nilay Patel and David Imel, who speak with AI researcher CJ Trowbridge about the state of running local LLMs on the Mac. Finally, it’s the long awaited return of the Thunder Round, as we race through stories so that Allison can make it to the airport. We’re chatting OpenAI math drama, digital ocarinas, and more.
